iPlan: Planning a Computer Game

Year 6, Lesson 3

steps.label: Today's Task
steps.content:
Today's Task

A computer program does not just get built - its behaviour gets planned first.

  • A plan describes what a game needs before anyone starts coding it.
  • Today you will plan your own Angry Birds style game, ready to build in a future lesson.
  • Your plan needs to be clear enough for someone else to build the game from it.

Key vocabulary

Design; plan; logical operators (greater than, less than, equal to); variables.

steps.label: Why Plan First?
steps.content:
Why Plan First?

A plan describes what a game needs before anyone starts building it.

  • Game studios split this work up: a designer plans the game, then a developer builds it from that plan.
  • If a plan is unclear, the developer cannot build the right game.
  • A good plan has to be clear enough for someone else, not just the person who wrote it, to follow.

Design vs plan

Designing is deciding what the game should be. Planning is writing that down clearly enough for someone else, or your future self, to build it from.

items.prompt: What is the real difference between designing and planning a game?
options: Designing decides what to build; planning writes it down
They mean exactly the same thing
Designing happens after the game is finished
Only the players of a finished game are allowed to plan it
items.explain: Designing is deciding what the game should be. Planning is writing that down clearly enough for someone else to build it from.

items.prompt: Why does a plan need to make sense to someone other than its writer?
options: A developer often builds the game from it
The writer will have forgotten it by the next lesson
Only teachers are allowed to read a plan
A plan is thrown away once it is read
items.explain: Game studios split this work up - a designer plans the game, then a developer builds it from that plan alone.

items.prompt: In a games studio, who usually writes the plan a developer builds from?
items.explain: The designer plans the game; the developer builds it from that plan.

steps.label: Meet Fly High!: On Your Marks
steps.content:
Meet Fly High!

Fly High! is a simplified Angry Birds style game, already built in Scratch from a plan just like the one you are about to write.

On your marks

when green flag clicked
glide (1) secs to x: (-184) y: (-93)
point in direction (90)

The bird sprite glides into its starting position and faces the right direction before anything else happens.

steps.label: Meet Fly High!: Get Set
steps.content:
Meet Fly High!: Get Set

ask [What angle, from my beak, should I fly at?] and wait
turn ccw (answer) degrees

The ask block is the player's input. Whatever they type is stored in answer, then used straight away to turn the bird.

steps.label: Meet Fly High!: Go!
steps.content:
Meet Fly High!: Go!

repeat until <touching [edge v]?> or <touching [Pig v]?>
move (3) steps
end

The bird keeps moving 3 steps at a time until one of two things becomes true: it reaches the edge of the screen, or it touches the Pig.

items.prompt: In Fly High!, what does the ask block store the player's typed answer in?
items.explain: The ask block always stores whatever the player types in a reporter called answer, ready to be used straight away.

items.prompt: What makes the bird in Fly High! stop moving?
options: Touching the edge, or touching the Pig
Pressing down the space bar to stop it moving
items.explain: The repeat until block keeps moving the bird until one of those two conditions becomes true.

items.prompt: Which block turns the bird based on what the player just typed?
items.explain: turn ccw uses answer, the value the ask block just stored, to decide how far to turn.

steps.label: Discuss the Game
steps.content:
Discuss the Game

Before writing your own plan, look closely at Fly High! and describe what you notice.

  • What are the sprites, and what does each one do?
  • How are the sprites interacting? For example, does the bird touching the pig score a point?
  • Do any sprites change costume?
  • What sounds does the game use?
  • What is the background?
  • What are the scores or levels?

Modelling a plan

Your teacher will start filling in a planning sheet on the board using Fly High! as the example, before you write your own.

steps.label: Check Your Understanding
steps.content:
Check Your Understanding

Questions to ask around the room:

  • Why do developers need a clear plan before they start building?
  • What is the difference between a sprite, a background, and a variable?
  • What must every game's plan include, at minimum?
  • What could go wrong if two developers worked from two different plans for the same game?

steps.label: Your Game Must Have
steps.content:
Plan Your Own Game

You are going to plan your own Angry Birds style game. Your plan must include:

Remember

A developer should be able to build your game from your plan alone - fill in every section on the next few slides.

steps.content:
Plan: Game and Aim

Game

What is its name?

Aim

What is the game's purpose?

steps.label: Plan: How It Ends
steps.content:
Plan: How It Ends

End

How do you win? How do you lose?

Backgrounds

Import an image, draw, or describe each one - at least one per level.

steps.label: Plan: Sprites
steps.content:
Plan: Sprites

What sprites will you need? In Fly High!, the Bird and the Pig were both sprites.

DescriptionWhat will it need to do?

What goes in the second column?

You do not need real code yet - just describe, in your own words, what you think that sprite will need to do.

steps.label: Plan: Variables
steps.content:
Plan: Variables

What variables will you need? Think back to score and speed from your Pong game.

NameDescription

steps.label: Review Your Plan
steps.content:
Review Your Plan

Everything you have written so far, pulled onto one screen.

steps.label: Extension: Swap and Explain
steps.content:
Extension: Swap and Explain

Swap devices with a partner and go back one slide to the Review screen - it shows their whole plan at once.

  1. Read your partner's plan on the Review screen.
  2. Explain, using only their plan, how you think their game will work.
  3. If anything is unclear, tell your partner - a plan that only makes sense to the person who wrote it is not finished yet.

Remember

Game developers often work from the plans of a completely different person, the game designer. If your plan only makes sense to you, a developer could not build it.

HarderTry increasing the complexity of your scoring rules, or adding more than two levels.
EasierIf you are stuck describing an idea in words, try drawing it instead and labelling the drawing.
